Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA)

ARIMA, short for AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average, is a powerful statistical model used to forecast time series data by capturing autocorrelations and trends.

ARIMA combines three key ideas:

  • AR (AutoRegressive): regression of the variable on its own lagged (past) values
  • I (Integrated): differencing of raw observations to make the time series stationary
  • MA (Moving Average): modeling of the error term as a linear combination of past error terms

An ARIMA(p, d, q) model consists of:

  • p: number of autoregressive (AR) terms
  • d: number of nonseasonal differences needed for stationarity
  • q: number of moving average (MA) terms

Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA)

When ARIMA has a seasonal component, it is referred to as SARIMA. In addition to non-seasonal components of order p, d and q, this model also contains seasonal components of order P, D and Q.

(Non-Seasonal) ARIMA + seasonal terms = Seasonal ARIMA

SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)m
(p,d,q) is non-seasonal component
(P,D,Q) is seasonal component
m is number of periods per season

where
- d = Number of lag differences
- p = Number of ordinary Autoregressive Lags
- q = Number of ordinary Moving average lags
- D = Number of seasonal differences
- P = Number of seasonal Autoregressive Lags
- Q = Number of seasonal Moving Average lags
- m = Seasonal period or number of observations per year

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_pacf, plot_acf
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, pacf

import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
from statsmodels.tsa.arima_process import ArmaProcess
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

Steps in Model Selection

  1. Check Stationarity
  2. Apply transformations, if needed
  3. Examine ACF, PACF
  4. Grid Search for ARIMA
  5. Fit ARIMA with lowest AIC
  6. Examine Residuals
  7. Forecast

Air Passengers Data

This dataset contains monthly air passenger counts for Ireland from 2010 to 2018. Our focus is on “international”, which is the number of international passengers in thousands.

passengers = pd.read_csv('air_passengers.csv', 
                 parse_dates = ['date'], date_format='%Y-%m-%d',
                 index_col='date')
passengers = passengers.loc[passengers.name =='Ireland',:]
passengers.columns = [col.lower() for col in passengers.columns]
passengers.head()
passengers = passengers.asfreq('MS')  # Specifies monthly frequency

Split Data

h = 12
train = passengers.iloc[:-h]
test = passengers.iloc[-h:]

1. Check for Stationarity

As discussed previously, a pre-requisite for the use of ARIMA is that the series be stationary. Stationarity can be tested
- Visual Examination of time series plot
- Statistical tests (e.g., Augmented Dickey Fuller)

print('ADF Test Statistic:', adfuller(train.international)[0])
print('p-value:', adfuller(train.international)[1])
print('-'*100)
train.international.plot()
plt.show()
ADF Test Statistic: 2.10841617491774
p-value: 0.9987982794721632
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Apply Tranformations

A non-stationary series can be made weakly stationary by

  • Stabilizing Variance
  • Seasonal Differencing
  • Lag Differencing
from scipy.stats import boxcox
boxcox_lambda = boxcox(train.international)[1]
print('Value of lambda to stabilize variance ', boxcox_lambda) 
print('-'*100)
international_boxcox = boxcox(train.international)[0]
transformed = pd.DataFrame({'international': train.international, 
                            'international_boxcox': international_boxcox},index = train.index)

print('ADF Test Statistic:', adfuller(transformed.international_boxcox)[0])
print('p-value:', adfuller(transformed.international_boxcox)[1])
print('-'*100)
transformed.international_boxcox.plot()
plt.show()
Value of lambda to stabilize variance  0.1251694035881738
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ADF Test Statistic: 2.497017976280054
p-value: 0.9990488826509608
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
transformed['international_boxcox_sdiff'] = transformed.international_boxcox.diff(12)
print('ADF Test Statistic:', adfuller(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff.dropna())[0])
print('p-value:', adfuller(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff.dropna())[1])
print('-'*100)
transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff.plot()
plt.show()
ADF Test Statistic: -1.9298091565702977
p-value: 0.318170463781791
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
transformed['international_boxcox_sdiff_diff'] = transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff.diff()
print('ADF Test Statistic:', adfuller(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff_diff.dropna())[0])
print('p-value:', adfuller(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff_diff.dropna())[1])
print('-'*100)
transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff_diff.plot()
plt.show()
ADF Test Statistic: -11.438962764313137
p-value: 6.246469499030272e-21
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Series was transformed by

  • boxcox transformation
  • 1 seasonal difference
  • 1 lag difference

3. Examine ACF and PACF

ACF and PACF plots are useful for identifying whether the data follows an AR, MA or ARMA process. In the case of AR and MA, it can help identify the order. For an ARMA process, these plots can offer hints or guidance on values of p, q, P and Q that may be good.

Examine PACF

pacf(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff_diff.dropna(), nlags = 24)
array([ 1.        , -0.38179545, -0.36576069, -0.2428943 , -0.13600033,
       -0.07762104, -0.23882328, -0.22004673,  0.00203172, -0.06315497,
       -0.05722584,  0.08102891, -0.13910396, -0.02415981,  0.03571549,
        0.00952263, -0.12882297, -0.06916871,  0.02862738,  0.00631009,
        0.20110304, -0.05526832, -0.11413771,  0.1375231 , -0.17580455])
plot_pacf(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff_diff.dropna(), lags=24)
plt.show()

Examine ACF

acf(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff_diff.dropna(),nlags=24)
array([ 1.        , -0.3771955 , -0.16266051,  0.04513516,  0.04905185,
       -0.00578219, -0.13452645,  0.04738344,  0.15790336, -0.10926659,
       -0.02696399,  0.10150151, -0.12930038,  0.06681487,  0.01061072,

        0.03160406, -0.09461414,  0.02563588,  0.08899322, -0.16338644])
plot_acf(transformed.international_boxcox_sdiff_diff.dropna(),lags=24)
plt.show()

Neither the PACF nor the ACF show a clear cut-off. Thus, both AR and MA processes are at work. Based on the PACF plot, it appears like p may be in the neighborhood of 3 and P is either 0, 1 or 2. Based on the ACF plot, it appears like q may be in the neighborhood of 2, while Q may be 0, 1 or 2.

4. Grid Search

An exhaustive search of all combinations of p, q, P and Q is likely to be extremely resource intensive. Therefore, we will use the PACF and ACF plot results to guide the choice of order values to test.

ARIMA has a mechanism to conduct differencing but not variance stabilization, so the latter must be done before the series is fed to ARIMA.

h = 12
train_lambda = boxcox(train.international)[1]
train.loc[:,['bc_international']] = boxcox(train.international)[0]
test.loc[:,['bc_international']] = boxcox(test.international, lmbda = train_lambda)
from itertools import product

# Stationarity Values and seasonality
d, D, s = 1, 1, 12

p_values = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
q_values = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
P_values = [0, 1, 2]
Q_values = [0, 1, 2]

results = []

for p, q, P, Q in product(p_values, q_values, P_values, Q_values):
    order = (p, d, q)
    seasonal_order = (P, D, Q, s)
    rec = {
        "order": order,
        "seasonal_order": seasonal_order,
        "aic": np.nan,
        "bic": np.nan,
        "converged": False
    }
    try:
        model = SARIMAX(
            train.bc_international,
            order=order,
            seasonal_order=seasonal_order,
            enforce_stationarity=True,
            enforce_invertibility=True,
            trend=None
        )
        fit = model.fit(disp=False, maxiter=200)
        rec["aic"] = fit.aic
        rec["bic"] = fit.bic
        rec["converged"] = fit.mle_retvals.get("converged", False)
    except Exception as e:
        rec["error"] = str(e)

    results.append(rec)

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("aic", na_position="last").reset_index(drop=True)

# Stationarity Values and seasonality
d, D, s = 1, 0, 12

p_values = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
q_values = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
P_values = [0]
Q_values = [0]

results = []

for p, q, P, Q in product(p_values, q_values, P_values, Q_values):
    order = (p, d, q)
    seasonal_order = (P, D, Q, s)
    rec = {
        "order": order,
        "seasonal_order": seasonal_order,
        "aic": np.nan,
        "bic": np.nan,
        "converged": False
    }
    try:
        model = SARIMAX(
            train.log_price,
            order=order,
            seasonal_order=seasonal_order,
            enforce_stationarity=True,

        rec["aic"] = fit.aic
        rec["bic"] = fit.bic
        rec["converged"] = fit.mle_retvals.get("converged", False)
    except Exception as e:
        rec["error"] = str(e)

    results.append(rec)

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("aic", na_position="last").reset_index(drop=True)
